title: AI and the EU Digital Markets Act: Addressing the Risks of Bigness in Generative AI
venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2023), PMLR 202
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the regulatory problem of how the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) should handle generative AI systems. The authors argue that the current DMA framework, which was designed for established digital platform services such as operating systems, web browsers, and social networking, does not explicitly cover generative AI even though such systems may become important gateways between business users and end users.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or empirical sample. Instead, it develops a legal and policy argument for treating certain generative AI services as “core platform services” under the DMA and for designating some AI developers as gatekeepers. It discusses how generative AI can function as a platform through products like ChatGPT and APIs, and it identifies sources of gatekeeping power such as computing resources, early-mover advantages, data resources, and integrated systems.

The authors conclude that the DMA should be amended or interpreted to prevent entrenched positions in generative AI markets and to support contestability, fairness, and diversity. The paper also sketches how specific DMA obligations could apply to generative AI providers, especially around data use, tying, and platform integration. No participant population, educational setting, or learning outcome is reported.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/policy position paper about the EU Digital Markets Act and generative AI market structure, not an empirical study of educational technology in schools. It contains no experimental, quasi-experimental, or observational evidence relevant to student outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no measured educational impact and does not evaluate ChatGPT use in middle school mathematics achievement or any student learning outcome. Its contribution is regulatory/theoretical rather than intervention-effect evidence.
